issues.legal_issue: A pure question of law based on undisputed or proven facts may be raised at a late appellate stage when entertaining it causes no unfair prejudice.
material_facts: The land-reform-law argument was raised for the first time in a Letters Patent Appeal.
The argument arose from the parties’ common case and depended on facts that had been found or were undisputed.
No unfair prejudice from considering the argument was established.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court was entitled to consider the new legal plea.
issues.legal_principle: A pure question of law going to the root of the case may be raised even in a court of last resort if it rests on admitted or proved facts and the opposing party is not taken by surprise or unfairly prejudiced. The Court relied on Connecticut Fire Insurance Company v. Kavanach, [1892] A.C. 473, 480.

rule.if: appeal_at_late_stage and pure_question_of_law and facts_undisputed_or_proven and not unfair_prejudice

predicates.appeal_at_late_stage: The matter is an appeal in which a party raises a legal plea at a late stage.
predicates.pure_question_of_law: The new plea raises a question of law rather than a dispute requiring new factual findings.
predicates.facts_undisputed_or_proven: The facts needed to decide the plea are admitted or established by the record.
predicates.unfair_prejudice: Allowing the plea would take the opposing party by surprise or otherwise unfairly prejudice that party.
predicates.late_legal_plea_may_be_considered: The court may consider the late legal plea.

issues.definition: When an appeal presents a pure legal issue on established facts and consideration would not unfairly prejudice the opposing party, the court may consider the late plea.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory saving for an intermediary’s khas possession requires actual possession, not merely a right to possess, and does not treat a hostile trespasser’s possession as the former owner’s possession.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed the suit lands under a partition that allotted them to him exclusively.
The contesting defendants were found to be in actual possession hostile to the plaintiff after dispossessing him before the notified vesting date.
The plaintiff relied on a right to possession and on constructive possession, rather than actual possession of the lands at vesting.
The case did not fall within the specifically included categories of lands treated as khas possession under the saving provision.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff was not in khas possession when vesting occurred, so the saving provision did not preserve his interest; his title to those lands vested in the State.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(k), 3, 4 and 6(1) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 distinguish actual, cultivatory khas possession from a mere right to possess. Section 6(1) expressly includes specified categories of lands otherwise outstanding with lessees or mortgagees, but does not extend to a former owner whose land is held adversely by a trespasser. The Court relied on Surajnath Ahir v. Prithinath Singh, [1963] 3 S.C.R. 290, and Ram Ran Bijai Singh v. Behari Singh, [1964] 3 S.C.R. 363, and rejected the contrary approach in Brij Nandan Singh v. Jamuna Prasad, A.I.R. 1958 Pat. 589.

rule.if: land_reform_vesting_case and former_owner_not_in_actual_possession_at_vesting and hostile_possessor_in_actual_control and not specifically_included_possession_category

predicates.land_reform_vesting_case: The proceeding concerns land affected by a statutory transfer of an intermediary’s interests to the State, subject to a possession-based saving.
predicates.former_owner_not_in_actual_possession_at: The former owner was not actually occupying or cultivating the land when the statutory transfer took effect.
predicates.hostile_possessor_in_actual_control: Another person had actual control of the land in opposition to the former owner.
predicates.specifically_included_possession_categor: The land falls within a category that the saving expressly treats as covered despite being outstanding with another person.
predicates.former_owner_not_entitled_to_retain_land: The former owner cannot retain the land under the possession-based saving.

issues.definition: Where a land-reform vesting case involves a former owner without actual possession at vesting and a hostile person in control, and no expressly included category applies, the former owner cannot retain the land under the saving.

issues.legal_issue: A voluntary partition or partition by deed may divide title between co-owners without the revenue procedure required to alter their land-revenue liability.
material_facts: The plaintiff and the other owners executed a partition deed dividing the properties by metes and bounds.
The plaintiff based his claim on the suit lands having been allotted to him exclusively by that partition.
The partition was not carried out through the procedure under the Estates Partition Act, 1897.
The plaintiff sued as exclusive owner, not as a co-sharer.
issues.conclusion: The partition was valid and divested the co-owners’ title in accordance with its terms; failure to follow the statutory revenue procedure affected land-revenue liability, not the validity of the division of title.
issues.legal_principle: The Estates Partition Act, 1897 protects land-revenue arrangements; it does not deprive co-owners or courts of the ability to divide property voluntarily or by decree. Its prescribed procedure is required to relieve parties from land-revenue liability attributable to another sharer’s land. The Court distinguished Mahanth Ram Bhushan Das v. Ramrati Kuer, 1965 Bihar L.J. 119, which concerned the effect of an amicable division on revenue administration.

predicates.civil_partition_claim: The proceeding concerns a claim to property based on a division among co-owners.
predicates.property_divided_by_voluntary_partition: The co-owners voluntarily divided the property, including by a deed specifying separate shares.
predicates.revenue_partition_procedure_not_followed: The parties did not follow the procedure prescribed for changing the revenue treatment of the divided holdings.
predicates.partition_divides_title_but_does_not_alt: The division may determine title between the co-owners but does not by itself alter their land-revenue liability.

issues.definition: When co-owners voluntarily divide property but do not follow the revenue procedure, the division may determine their title while leaving revenue liability unchanged.

issues.legal_issue: The civil court’s jurisdiction to decide title and a consequential claim for possession is not excluded merely because the land-reform statute provides for possession-related action by revenue authorities.
material_facts: The plaintiff brought a civil suit for declaration of title and possession.
The High Court rejected the plaintiff’s title under the land-reform statute without investigating possession as a matter for revenue authorities.
The provisions relied on did not expressly prohibit a civil court from deciding title and the consequential right to possession.
issues.conclusion: The civil court’s jurisdiction to decide title and consequential possession was not barred.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 6(1), 6(2) and 35 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 contain no express or inferable prohibition against a civil court deciding title and the consequential right to possession. The Court found that section 35 dealt with different kinds of suits.

predicates.civil_title_and_possession_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit seeking a decision on title and consequential possession.
predicates.statute_contains_no_express_or_implied_b: The applicable statutory scheme does not expressly or by necessary implication exclude civil adjudication of those claims.
predicates.civil_court_may_adjudicate_title_and_con: The civil court may decide title and the consequential claim for possession.

issues.definition: In a civil title-and-possession suit, the civil court may decide those claims if the applicable statutory scheme does not exclude that adjudication.

issues.legal_issue: A criminal court’s declaration of a party’s actual possession, without an order transferring possession, does not by itself deprive that party of the legal benefit of its possession.
material_facts: A proceeding concerning possession had taken place before a Magistrate.
The Magistrate declared that the contesting defendants were in actual possession but did not direct that possession be handed over to them.
The plaintiff argued that the defendants should not benefit from possession associated with the Magistrate’s order.
issues.conclusion: The Magistrate’s order supplied no basis for disregarding the defendants’ actual possession or the consequences that the land-reform statute attached to it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that an order declaring actual possession, rather than directing delivery of possession, did not confer an unjust advantage or create a principle for withholding a benefit that otherwise arose under the statute.

predicates.civil_possession_dispute: The matter is a civil dispute in which the parties’ possession of land is relevant.
predicates.magistrate_declared_actual_possession: A Magistrate recorded that a party was in actual possession of the land.
predicates.magistrate_did_not_order_transfer: The Magistrate did not direct that possession be delivered to that party.
predicates.declared_possession_not_disregarded_mere: The party’s declared actual possession is not disregarded merely because of the Magistrate’s order.

issues.definition: Where a Magistrate records actual possession without ordering a transfer, that possession is not disregarded merely because it was recorded in the Magistrate’s proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A person found in possession of land vested in the State does not obtain a right or equity to retain it merely by becoming liable to pay rent under the rules.
material_facts: The suit lands vested in the State, and the plaintiff was outside the statutory category of former owners whose possession was saved.
The contesting defendants were found to be trespassers in possession.
The rule relied on provided for rent or ground-rent to be payable by a person found in possession after the outgoing proprietor was found not to have been in possession.
issues.conclusion: The rule imposed rent liability on a person in possession but did not confer a right or equity to remain in possession; the State could seek direct possession through its revenue authorities.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4(f) and 4(g) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 assign the Collector duties concerning lands vested in the State and provide a mechanism for requiring delivery of possession. Rule 7-H of the Rules creates liability to pay rent or ground-rent for a person found in possession; it does not grant that person a right to retain possession.

predicates.land_vested_in_state: The land has passed to the State under a statutory vesting process.
predicates.possessor_not_within_saved_owner_categor: The person in possession is not within a category whose former ownership or possession is preserved by the statutory scheme.
predicates.possessor_found_in_control: A person has been found in actual control of the land.
predicates.rent_liability_does_not_create_right_to_: Liability to pay rent does not itself create a right to retain land vested in the State.

issues.definition: When land has vested in the State and a person outside the saved-owner category is found in control, rent liability alone does not give that person a right to retain the land.

issues.legal_issue: A plaintiff may obtain possession against defendants who disclaim possession of particular plots where the plaintiff’s title against them is established, without affecting the rights of the State or a third party.
material_facts: The plaintiff had established title to the scheduled properties as against both sets of defendants before the statutory vesting issue arose.
The contesting defendants admitted that they had no possession of or connection with certain plots and asserted that those plots had been made over to the other defendants.
The State’s rights after vesting and any third party’s possession were not adjudicated.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff was granted possession of the plots identified in the defendants’ admission, subject to the rights of the State and any third party remaining unaffected.
issues.legal_principle: Where the defendants against whom relief is sought admit that they do not possess particular property, the plaintiff may obtain possession if title against those defendants is established and the other defendants possess the property or no one does. The decree binds only the litigating parties and does not prejudice the State or third parties.

predicates.civil_property_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit seeking relief concerning property.
predicates.plaintiff_established_title_against_defe: The plaintiff established title to the property as against the defendants from whom relief is sought.
predicates.defendants_admit_no_possession_of_specif: Those defendants admit that they do not possess or claim a connection with particular plots.
predicates.state_or_third_party_rights_not_adjudica: The rights of the State or a third party in the plots have not been determined in the suit.
predicates.possession_decree_may_issue_against_defe: The court may grant possession against the defendants while leaving nonparties’ rights unaffected.

issues.definition: Where title against the defendants is established and they admit they do not possess particular plots, a possession decree may issue against them without determining nonparties’ rights.

issues.legal_issue: A trespasser’s liability for mesne profits against the former owner ends when the former owner’s title is extinguished by statutory vesting, and liability is limited to property the trespasser possessed.
material_facts: The defendants dispossessed the plaintiff and possessed some of the suit lands wrongfully before the statutory vesting date.
The plaintiff’s title was extinguished by the statutory vesting because the possession-based saving did not apply.
The contesting defendants admitted that they had not possessed certain plots.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff was entitled to mesne profits only up to the date of vesting and only for the items found to have been in the contesting defendants’ possession.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 4 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 transferred the relevant interests to the State on vesting. The Court limited the former owner’s mesne-profit award to the period before that transfer and to the land actually possessed by the defendants.

predicates.civil_mesne_profits_claim: The proceeding includes a claim for mesne profits arising from wrongful possession of property.
predicates.defendant_wrongfully_possessed_property_: The defendant wrongfully possessed the property before a statutory transfer of ownership took effect.
predicates.plaintiff_title_ended_at_vesting: The plaintiff’s title ended when the statutory transfer took effect.
predicates.mesne_profits_limited_to_prevesting_peri: Mesne profits are limited to the period before the transfer and to property the defendant possessed.

issues.definition: When wrongful possession preceded a statutory transfer that ended the plaintiff’s title, mesne profits are limited to the pre-transfer period and to property possessed by the defendant.
